summary: In some machine-to-machine scenarios the server's response to a client request is redundant. This informational document defines a CoAP option that lets a client say it is not interested in responses, minimizing resource use in constrained systems that update many resources or send data at a high rate.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you shout instructions to many helpers and do not need each to say okay. This gives tiny devices a way to say please do not reply, saving their energy.

questions: when should i use no-response in coap
what does value 26 mean in no-response
subtitle: Skip server responses for less-critical CoAP requests to save power and bandwidth.

tldr.problem: In machine-to-machine systems, constrained devices may need to send frequent updates or commands where server responses are redundant and just waste bandwidth and battery.
tldr.mechanism: The No-Response option in CoAP lets a client explicitly tell the server it does not want responses, or only wants certain classes of responses (like errors), and the server may suppress them.
tldr.outcome: Constrained systems can dramatically reduce traffic, server load, and battery drain when responses are not needed—especially useful for high-frequency updates like vehicle telemetry or multicast commands.

today: RFC 7967 is Informational and remains the specification for the CoAP No-Response option. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is designed for devices with very limited power and bandwidth. Normally, when a CoAP client sends a request, the server always responds with a status code, even if the client does not care about the response.

This document introduces the No-Response option. A client can add this option to a request to tell the server: 'I don't want a response' or 'I only want responses if something goes wrong.' The server can then skip sending the response, saving battery power on both ends and reducing network congestion.

This is particularly valuable in machine-to-machine (M2M) scenarios where a device updates many resources at once or sends data very frequently. Responses just waste bandwidth and drain batteries.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending out a flood of tasks and being okay if nobody replies—just assume everything worked. This option tells servers 'don't bother replying unless there's an error.'

sections.title: The No-Response Option and Granular Control
sections.content:
The No-Response option is assigned CoAP option number 258. It is a request option (added to a request, not a response) and is optional and not repeatable.

The option contains a bitmap value that gives granular control over which response classes the client wishes to suppress:

  • Value 0 (empty): interested in all responses (default).
  • Value 2: not interested in success responses (2.xx class, like 2.04 Changed).
  • Value 8: not interested in client error responses (4.xx class, like 4.04 Not Found).
  • Value 16: not interested in server error responses (5.xx class, like 5.03 Service Unavailable).

These can be combined using bitwise OR. For example, value 18 means 'suppress 2.xx and 5.xx, but send 4.xx errors back.' Value 26 suppresses all responses.

When using value 26 (suppress everything), a client should stop listening for responses. If the client wants to see any error responses, it must continue listening during a timeout period because it cannot tell if no response means success or loss.
sections.eli5: The option is like a checklist: 'Don't tell me about successes, do tell me about errors.' Different checkboxes let you control which types of messages you want back.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
The No-Response option works well for two main application scenarios.

First, frequent location updates from vehicles: A vehicle with a GPS sensor can use Non-confirmable (NON) messages to send location updates to a backend server every 20 seconds. Since the vehicle is constantly moving, past coordinates are already stale. Asking the server to respond would generate millions of unnecessary messages from all the vehicles. With No-Response set to value 26 (suppress all), the traffic drops dramatically.

Second, multicast commands to appliances: A smart-home controller sends a command to turn on all lights in a building using a single multicast message. Without No-Response, every light would respond, congesting the network. With No-Response set to suppress success responses but allow errors (using value 2), only lights that failed would reply, making it easy to spot problems.

The RFC notes that servers may decide to suppress responses; they are not required to. The option is advisory—a server can ignore it if it needs to.
sections.eli5: Picture sending 'update location' commands to thousands of cars, or 'turn on lights' to hundreds of rooms. Asking each one to reply wastes tons of bandwidth. This option lets you tell them 'just do it, and only say something if you fail.'

sections.title: Implementation Challenges
sections.content:
Several practical issues arise when using No-Response.

Token reuse: CoAP uses tokens to match requests to responses. When No-Response is used, a response may never arrive, so the client must decide when it is safe to reuse the token for a new request. The RFC recommends waiting at least NON_LIFETIME + MAX_SERVER_RESPONSE_DELAY + MAX_LATENCY seconds, or using a unique token for each request.

Congestion control: When No-Response is used with NON messages, there is no feedback from the server. The client loses the ability to detect congestion through response timing. The RFC therefore recommends a minimum 3-second interval between updates and suggests occasionally sending regular requests (without No-Response) to get feedback and confirm the server is still responding.

Caching: Responses triggered by No-Response requests can still be cached. If a response is cacheable, it must be cached even though the client did not ask for it.

The option is Unsafe-to-Forward, meaning intermediaries that don't understand it should not forward the request, since they would otherwise wait for a response that never comes.
sections.eli5: There are gotchas: when is it safe to send another request with the same token? How do you know if the server is still working if you never get replies? The RFC gives careful guidance for each.

items.label: (empty)
items.desc: Interested in all responses (default, no suppression).

items.label: Suppress 4.xx
items.desc: Do not send client error responses.

items.label: Suppress 5.xx
items.desc: Do not send server error responses.

items.label: Suppress all
items.desc: Completely one-way communication; do not expect any response.
